article_title: Clinical decision-making skill in diagnosing of oral diseases among medical interns.
citation: Farzan Ava, Heidarzadeh Abtin, Nemati Shadman, Khoshrang Hossein, Basirat Maryam. (2026). Clinical decision-making skill in diagnosing of oral diseases among medical interns. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09589-7
title: A 19-item Key Feature-based oral disease diagnostic assessment instrument with Delphi validation and killer options
description: An assessment instrument of "19 case-based Key Feature questions to assess critical steps in diagnostic reasoning," most accompanied by visual aids, covering common oral diseases of varying diagnostic complexity. Items were derived from an expert disease list via a two-round Delphi process with ≥ 80% agreement predefined. Scoring awards credit only when all essential options are identified, and selecting predefined unsafe "killer" options loses credit for the item. Reliability and validity were quantified (Cronbach's alpha = 0.70; ICC = 0.861; CVR 0.53–1.00; CVI 0.84–1.00).
requirements: Requires expert panel consensus (two-round Delphi, ≥ 80% agreement) to define key features and the scoring rubric and answer key
Requires two faculty raters scoring independently with discrepancy resolution through discussion
constraints: The authors caution that the high test–retest values may partly reflect the short 10-day retest interval and sample homogeneity and were interpreted cautiously
target_learning_goals: Clinical decision-making and diagnostic reasoning for oral diseases
examples: The instrument was administered online to 66 interns at Guilan University of Medical Sciences between March 2023 and February 2024, with raw scores rescaled to a 0–20 scale.
key_sources: Farzan Ava, Heidarzadeh Abtin, Nemati Shadman, Khoshrang Hossein, Basirat Maryam. (2026). Clinical decision-making skill in diagnosing of oral diseases among medical interns. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09589-7

article_title: Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students.
citation: Mehrdad M, Jambarsang S, Sadeghian H, Jabinian F, Keshmiri F. (2025). Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334545
title: Key Features examination and WHOBARS checklist for assessing reasoning and performance in patient safety education
description: The study used two instruments: a paper-based Key Features examination (15 questions, each with one scenario and 12 options from which students chose three; scoring range 0–45) to assess reasoning in managing patient safety incidents, validated by 15 experts; and the WHOBARS behavioral rating scale covering Sign-In, Time-Out, and Sign-Out, each with five items scored 1 (poor) to 7 (excellent), total range 15–105. "The psychometrics of the mentioned instrument were approved by the authors (Cronbach's Alpha 0.86, ICC = 0.81)" for WHOBARS.
requirements: A trained, blinded evaluator conducting a minimum of three independent observations per participant per time point
constraints: WHOBARS was designed by Devcich et al. (2016) for three strategic surgery times; performance scores were derived as the mean of three observational assessments per time point
target_learning_goals: Assessment of clinical reasoning in patient safety incident management and of checklist-based surgical safety performance
examples: Performance was evaluated across Sign-In, Time-Out, and Sign-Out phases during patient safety–specific scenarios at baseline, two weeks, and two months
key_sources: Mehrdad M, Jambarsang S, Sadeghian H, Jabinian F, Keshmiri F. (2025). Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334545

article_title: Thinking About the Why: A Qualitative Study on Students' Perspectives of Paediatric Team-Based Learning Discussions.
citation: N. Mitchell, M. Rashid, J. Foulds, and K. Forbes. (2025). Thinking About the Why: A Qualitative Study on Students' Perspectives of Paediatric Team‐Based Learning Discussions. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70161
title: Key-feature-question-based team-based learning session for paediatric clinical reasoning
description: A modified TBL session within the paediatric clerkship that employs key-feature questions to focus on clinical decision-making. "The TBL session occurs once per rotation and involves six clinical scenarios, each with two to four associated KFQs to focus on clinical decision‐making." Students first commit to answers individually in an IRAT, then reach group consensus in a GRAT in small groups of four to five, followed by a facilitated discussion giving real-time feedback on rationales and alternate responses. The 2-h session was held online during the COVID-19 pandemic at the time of the study.
requirements: Small groups of four to five students completing the same six scenarios individually (IRAT) then as a group (GRAT)
A facilitated discussion articulating key features and rationales for correct and incorrect responses
constraints: The study version was delivered virtually because of the COVID-19 pandemic; sessions have since returned to in-person
target_learners: third-year medical students in an 8-week mandatory paediatric clerkship
examples: The session blueprint (Appendix 1) spans six clinical problems from conjugated jaundice in an infant to weight loss in an adolescent, covering diagnosis, history, investigations, physical exam and management key features
key_sources: N. Mitchell, M. Rashid, J. Foulds, and K. Forbes. (2025). Thinking About the Why: A Qualitative Study on Students' Perspectives of Paediatric Team‐Based Learning Discussions. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70161
